articles.headline: The ESA’s Euclid Telescope Discovered a New Comet Completely by Accident
keyFacts: The European Space Agency's Euclid telescope accidentally discovered a new comet named C/2026 S1 (Euclid) located 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth.
Researchers including Mikko Pöntinen found the comet using custom software that flagged a moving object while the telescope was aimed away from the solar system's plane.
Astronomers stated the long-period comet likely originated from the Oort Cloud and is expected to reach its closest point to the sun in 2027.
body: Approximately 40 to 70 new comets are discovered every year, most of which are found by astronomers actively looking for comets or at least new celestial bodies in general. But at least one comet discovered in 2026 doesn’t have that distinction. It was discovered entirely by accident by a telescope that was not actively looking for comets.

Say hello to C/2026 S1 (Euclid), a brand new comet that was just discovered by the European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope. The comet is located about 1.3 billion kilometers away from Earth, which is roughly the distance between the sun and the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. It was discovered by Mikko Pöntinen of the University of Helsinki, together with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group, who were using the Euclid telescope at the time of discovery.

What makes this one weird, among the thousands of other comets humans have named, is how they found it. The group was intentionally pointing the telescope away from the elliptical plane, a band in the sky where the solar system’s planets, most of its asteroids and a significant number of its comets reside. The idea was to avoid the cosmic dust and debris left behind by those celestial bodies, allowing the group to take clearer pictures of distant galaxies in deep space.
More from CNET

While doing this, a comet zipped through. It could have gone entirely unnoticed, but Pöntinen had written software to identify moving objects, which flagged images where the comet appeared. Pöntinen was then able to use its speed and trajectory to find it in other images and report it as a new comet.

“I was excited to see my software flag a ‘streak’ smeared across several images,” Pöntinen said in a statement. “Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.”
A happy coincidence
The most interesting part of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) is undoubtedly that it was discovered by a telescope that wasn’t designed to find comets on a mission that also wasn’t designed to find comets.

According to Bruno Altieri, archive scientist and member of the Euclid solar system team, this is because of the way the Euclid telescope works. It spends most of its time in a wide survey that will eventually map about one-third of the extragalactic sky, which encompasses all the planets, radiation clouds, debris clouds and other structures outside of the Milky Way galaxy.

It also employs a “step-and-stare” method of mapping the cosmos, which means it “steps” to a spot, stares at the sky for about an hour and then moves on. That means much of what it looks at is only looked at once. Since comets are often found thanks to their movement, it’s hard to identify such an object with this observation method.

Euclid also conducts a deep field survey. These are zoomed-in glimpses of specific parts of space conducted periodically around the schedule of the wide survey. These parts are revisited only a handful of times per year, and that’s the only reason C/2026 S1 (Euclid) was discovered.
“This discovery is indeed a happy coincidence as few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid,” Altieri said.
Straight up from the sun

Very little is known about C/2026 S1 (Euclid) so far, as it’s only been imaged a few times. There are a few things that astronomers have already gleaned from what they have seen. For starters, this is a long-period comet, which means its orbit around the sun lasts more than 200 years. The exact time hasn’t been calculated, but early estimates put it at thousands of years before it completes a full orbit.

According to Altieri, that means it almost certainly came from the Oort Cloud, which is a shell of icy bodies, rocky planetesimals and other debris that surrounds the entire solar system. Comets from the Oort Cloud are referred to as “nearly isotropic” comets and orbit the sun from all sorts of zany angles. C/2026 S1 (Euclid) is no different.

Space doesn’t have an up or down, but if it did, C/2026 S1 (Euclid) would be straight up from the sun as viewed from Earth. Its sweeping orbit takes it far above the solar system before cutting between Saturn and Jupiter on its way back down. It’s expected to reach perihelion — the point where it’s closest to the sun — in 2027. After that, it won’t be back there for thousands of years.

articles.headline: The Trump administration’s evolving Starshield deflection
keyFacts: U.S. officials and Elon Musk provided conflicting explanations regarding recent speed reductions in Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield connectivity.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the U.S. government ordered the slowdowns, which reduced connectivity fivefold and impacted Ukraine's counter-drone defenses.
Bipartisan U.S. senators requested an Inspector General investigation into the connectivity slowdowns while envoys planned trilateral peace talks.
body: President Donald Trump and other senior U.S. officials have given a range of explanations, some of which appeared contradictory, for Ukraine’s SpaceX-related connectivity disruptions earlier this week.

The collection of Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio , Secretary of War Pete Hegseth , and Republican donor and SpaceX founder Elon Musk have offered a variety of confusing statements about who ultimately was the final decision-maker behind a choice that Ukrainians feel like resulted in civilian casualties.

This ongoing dispute began last week when Ukrainian leaders announced their access to Starlink and Starshield connectivity had been slowed. They use Starlink and the non-commercially available Starshield to communicate quickly and to launch and defend against drone attacks.
Marco Rubio:

Speaking from Mumbai, India, on Wednesday, Rubio said, “Suffice it to say that the reporting out there was that somehow the United States government was denying them something they needed in order to defend their country. That’s not true. That’s not accurate. And for leaders in Ukraine to continue to represent that is also not accurate.

“The bottom line is that [this] is governed by a private commercial contract as to the – how their stuff can be used and what speeds they allow it to be used at,” he said. “And so we’ll continue to engage on the matter, but the reporting initially was that somehow this was part of a directive from the United States Government, and I’m just here to tell you, as I’ve said repeatedly from the very beginning and the President has made clear, at no point did he say deny them the use of this system because I’m trying to punish them or teach them a lesson.”
Pete Hegseth:
Like Rubio, Hegseth said during an unrelated trip to Ohio on Tuesday, the department’s “policy hasn’t changed” with regard to Ukraine.

“There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions. But nothing’s changed from our view; we haven’t made any directives or anything like that,” he said.

Hegseth’s remarks appear to differ from the department’s stance regarding Anthropic, the company that created the artificial intelligence chatbot Claude. While Anthropic wanted to ensure the department formally agreed to specific use requirements, the Pentagon refused, arguing that it would not let private companies dictate to the military how it would use its equipment as long as it fell within legal guardrails.
Elon Musk:

Their comments appear to put the onus of this on SpaceX, or at least deflect the administration from the decision, though Musk has already denied that SpaceX played a role in the plan. The entrepreneur said last week Starshield is “owned and controlled by the US government” and “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”
In prior posts, he has explained that Starlink is for civilian use and is not allowed to be used for offensive military operations, while Starshield was built for and is operated by the government.

“Once again, important to emphasize that there are two different systems: Starlink for civilian usage and Starshield that is built & operated for US govt,” he said in May. “We try hard to keep these separate.”
Donald Trump:
Last week, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn, “I don’t know if it was anybody, because it wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon.”

To add to the confusion over who was ultimately responsible for the decision, the Wall Street Journal reported it came from Musk, but even the outlet’s own sources disputed whether Musk acted unilaterally. Reuters , for its part, reported that the decision came from the White House, though it did not specify whether that meant the president ordered it or another White House official.
Volodymyr Zelensky:
Zelensky, in a Fox News interview on Wednesday morning, said Ukraine’s connectivity had slowed fivefold and warned that it had a direct impact on its counter-drone measures.

“The message came from government,” Zelensky said in a weekend interview on Meet the Press , pointing the blame on the administration. “I don’t know from whom, what cabinet, and et cetera. And I think it doesn’t work either way. I don’t know, really. But it’s not my opinion. It’s opinion of our generals, of our government, and of course my also opinion, that it was a message from American government to limit the speed. And technically, SpaceX did it.”

The Starshield debacle is happening at a time when the president is making other overtures to Russia, primarily related to oil sanctions relief, while intensifying his criticism of Zelensky. Over the last week or so, Trump has called on Zelensky to step down and accused him of trying to prolong the war.

Zelensky has also claimed that the Ukrainian military had not recently received early warning alerts about incoming attacks, which have also resulted in unnecessary casualties. He said in the Wednesday television interview that the early warnings have since been restored.

In the Meet the Press interview, the Ukrainian president said the United States has “this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles, and we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”
The sanctions relief decision was widely criticized by members of both parties on Capitol Hill, as was the Starshield slowdown.

A bipartisan group of senators requested the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General investigate the Starshield connectivity issue, while another group of lawmakers sought additional information from SpaceX. The Pentagon’s IG has not announced whether it would begin an investigation.

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner, who is Trump’s son-in-law, and Steve Witkoff, Trump’s longtime friend, have led the administration’s negotiating efforts, and they most recently met with Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday and in St. Petersburg, Russia, to meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin .
‘CHANGES THE BALANCE OF LEVERAGE’: ZELENSKY TRIES TO HOLD ON AS TRUMP PRESSURES HIM TO CONCEDE

“These discussions were constructive, and will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level,” Witkoff wrote on social media. “While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end and achieving a comprehensive, durable peace that will provide security and prosperity for generations to come.”
The episode has devolved the Trump-Zelensky relationship to its lowest point since Trump threw Zelensky out of the Oval Office last year.

The Starlink debacle raises broader concerns about overreliance on a single platform or weapon, a situation rife with the possibility of unintended consequences should there be any hiccups in the supply chain support or infrastructure of the platform.

The ongoing tension between Trump and Zelensky also pertains to recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which the Trump administration has said is a contributing factor to rising energy prices globally and could hurt them in next month’s midterm elections. Zelensky offered to stop such attacks if the U.S. gave it the needed intelligence to target their missile launchers deep within Russian territory.

articles.headline: Democrats have 11-point lead among likely voters as Trump’s approval rating craters – live
keyFacts: Likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans by 11 percentage points, according to New York Times and Siena University polling.
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion penalty after a jury found it deceived users about data privacy.
Donald Trump will continue his campaign blitz in South Carolina for Republican Senate nominee Darline Graham before the midterm elections.
body: Democrats have 11-point lead among likely voters as Trump’s approval rating craters – live
New poll finds likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points; Trump campaigns in South Carolina
New polling shows likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans, fewer than two weeks until midterm elections
New polling from the New York Times and Siena University shows that likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points.
Meanwhile, Donald Trump’s approval rating dropped to a new low for this particular survey – 36%.

Notably, according to the Times’ polling, the perception of either party has shifted over the last two years. The number of people who consider Democrats as the party of the working class has grown by five points – from 48% to 53%, while it’s dropped by five points for Republicans – from 45% to 40%.
Musk threatens to 'come for' Democrats who 'pick fights' with him in new Congress
Elon Musk – the tech billionaire, Trump ally, and founder of Tesla and Space X – has threatened to home in on Democrats who pursue him in the next Congress.

“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” Musk wrote on X, the social media platform he bought in 2022. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.”

This comes after Politico reported earlier today that Democratic lawmakers were considering how best to investigate Musk, and his businesses, if the party gains control of Congress following the midterm elections.

US envoy Steve Witkoff announced this morning that Russia authorities had freed Stephen Hubbard, the first American known to be convicted of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Hubbard was arrested when the Russians briefly took over the Ukrainian city of Izium at the start of the ongoing conflict in 2022.

Donald Trump welcomed the news,noting the prisoner release was the result of a direct request he made to Putin in a telephone call last week. Meanwhile, after Witkoff’s discussions with Putin in St Petersburg, he flattered the Russian president by calling him a “humanitarian”. The emissary’s comments drew bipartisan backlash, but Trump defended them: “I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out,” the US president told reporters in the East Room.

Witkoff also said that his discussions with Putin were “constructive”, and“will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia and Ukraine at the technical level”. This comes after Trump’s reignited feud with Zelenskyy after he urged Kyiv to end its attacks on Russian refineries and waived sweeping sanctions against Moscow.

New polling from the New York Times and Siena University shows thatlikely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points. Meanwhile, Trump’s approval rating dropped to a new low for this particular survey – 36%.

At a campaign rally in Cincinnati, Ohio, JD Vance criticized the media and Democrats for focusing on Vivek Ramaswamy’s recent ad for his gubernatorial campaign, which features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent,Amy Acton. The vice-president defended Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar”. Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, claimed in the spot that her daughter “lied her entire life” about living in a tent during her childhood. However, Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, said on Tuesday that his sister is estranged from her mother, who had married a man that sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old. Arthur, he said, remained in the marriage even after her husband was arrested and her children were taken away from her.

The supreme court has refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately deny gender-affirming care for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy while a legal challenge plays out. It was adopted after an executive order from Trump, who’s taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.

With 13 days until the midterms,Trump will continue his campaign blitz by heading to Clemson, South Carolina, where he’ll rally for Darline Graham – the Republican nominee for US Senate who is hoping to secure a full term for her late brother’s seat. Darline was appointed by the South Carolina governor to carry out the remainder of Lindsey Graham’s time in office after his death in July. However, she now faces a competitive race against Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and the Democratic nominee, in a contest that has become increasingly rancorous in recent months.
Trump defends special envoy Witkoff calling Putin a 'humanitarian'
In the East Room today, Trump defended Steve Witkoff’s comments, noting that the release of Steven Hubbard might warrant praise for Putin.
“I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out,” Trump told reporters.

Earlier, we noted that Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, slammed special envoy Steve Witkoff for calling Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” today – following the release of detained US citizen Steven Hubbard.
Now, more GOP lawmakers are pushing back.
“Vladimir Putin is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian,” said retiring Republican senator Joni Ernst.
She added: “His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life. Appeasement won’t end this war. Pressure will.”

With 13 days until the midterms, early voting data is rolling in nationwide. Democrats need to net four Senate seats and hold 218 House seats to reclaim a congressional majority. Here is where the numbers stand so far:

Turnout is surging in key battlegrounds: Over 16 million Americans have already voted in person or by mail. According to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, battleground states -including Michigan, Ohio, Georgia, Texas, Florida and North Carolina – have each passed 700,000 ballots cast as of 21 October. Turnout is being driven in part by widespread voter frustration, reflected in Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings.

Democrats lead in early returns: Registered Democrats account for 47% of early ballots cast, compared with 29% from Republicans (tracking returned ballots, not candidate selection). The party gap is most pronounced in North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa. While Republicans traditionally favor election day voting, strategists worry this widened margin signals a “red undertow” – GOP voters staying home due to frustration over high gas prices, the conflict in Iran and sweeping tariffs.

Early votes are pacing well ahead of 2022: In Georgia, early votes already represent nearly 30% of the total turnout from the 2022 midterms. Florida sits at 18%, with similarly high paces recorded in North Carolina, Michigan and Ohio.

Mail-in voting remains resilient: Over 56m mail-in ballots have been requested or sent nationally – greater than the 52m requested in 2022, according to NBC News (using data from TargetSmart). Despite executive orders from the Trump administration attempting to restrict mail-in voting, which the supreme court struck down in September, voters continue to utilize the process at pre-pandemic rates.
Meta ordered to pay $25bn penalty over deceiving users about data privacy

A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn in penalties, on after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that Cambridge Analytica – a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign – obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.

The state’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219bn was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25bn.

In Maine, Susan Collins, the moderate Republican incumbent senator vying for a sixth term in office, joined the growing list of GOP lawmakers to urge the Trump administration to reverse the waiving of Russian sanctions.

“First of all the law is very clear, that we wanted additional sanctions to be imposed on Russia, by cutting the deal on diesel with Russia. [Trump] is not going to increase the supply to the United States in any measurable way. But what he is going to do is to get more funding for Russia to use to attack Ukraine,” Collins told reporters in Lewiston, where she was joined by former independent senator Joe Manchin for a campaign stop.
Vance criticizes outrage over Ramaswamy ad featuring opponent's estranged mother

At a campaign rally in Cincinnati, Ohio, JD Vance criticized the media and Democrats for focusing on Vivek Ramaswamy’s recent ad for his gubernatorial campaign, which features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

As we noted earlier, the campaign spot, which has circulated among conservatives on social media, shows Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, claiming that her daughter “lied her entire life” about spending time living in a tent during her childhood.

However, Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, blasted the ad, and said his sister is estranged from her mother, who had married a man that sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old. Arthur, he said, remained in the marriage even after her husband was arrested and her children were taken away from her.
Today, Vance defended Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it isand calls Amy Acton a liar”.
Vance added: “My message, ladies and gentlemen, is very simple. Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts.”
Witkoff calls meeting with Putin 'constructive', says trilateral talks will continue 'at the technical level'

Special envoy Steve Witkoff said his meeting today with Vladimir Putin – which resulted in the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails– was “constructive”.

Trump’s emissary met with Russian leadership in St Petersburg, after talks in Oslo with Zelenskyy and Nordic leaders. The Ukrainian president has pushed for an in-person meeting with Moscow and Washington to hammer out a lasting peace deal, as fighting rages on.
Witkoff added that his discussions today “will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia and Ukraine at the technical level”.

“While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end and achieving a comprehensive, durable peace that will provide security and prosperity for generations to come,” Witkoff said, following the president’s reignited feud with Zelenskyy after he urged Kyiv to end its attacks on Russian refineries and waived sweeping sanctions against Moscow.
A 24-year-old Kansas man has been arrested for allegedly threatening to shoot Donald Trump.

Authorities arrested Jaden J Read, of Clearwater, Kansas, last Saturday after he allegedly posted threats to kill the US president at his rally in the Wichita area on Monday, according to the justice department.

According to federal authorities, a Crime Stoppers tip on 15 October led investigators to a Facebook post responding to a KAKE News article about Trump’s upcoming Wichita visit. Read allegedly commented: “Let’s shoot Trump honestly, where’s our shooter? I’m tired of living this money life.”
Immediately afterward, he allegedly posted a second comment on the same article: “I just got a 308 and 305 round and I’m killing this pedo.”
Authorities also found two additional comments allegedly posted by Read in response to a KWCH 12 News article about Trump’s planned visit.

“Can we shoot him in Kansas please I will myself,” Read allegedly wrote. A minute later, he allegedly posted another comment, saying: “IK where your speech will be. Already mapped out roofs around. Finna get kirked since yall couldn’t help him.”

Read was arrested in Clearwater last Saturday and taken into federal custody, where he will remain pending a detention hearing. The district of Kansas filed a criminal complaint against Read for making threats against the president.
Retiring GOP senator Thom Tillis has ridiculed DonaldTrump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff for praising Vladimir Putinas a “humanitarian”.
“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis said in a post on X, with a screenshot showing the definition.

“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” the North Carolina senator went on. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”

Elena Kagan criticized rulings made by the US supreme court’s conservative majority this week, arguing that its recent decisions on redistricting and campaign finance had undermined America’s democracy.

“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works,” said Kagan, one of the court’s three liberal justices, during a discussion at Catholic University’s law school in Washington DC yesterday, according to multiple reports.
She emphasized that the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, “has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should”.

Kagan’s remarks come just two weeks before the midterm elections and amid battles over congressional redistricting. Earlier this year, the supreme court struck down Louisiana’s congressional map, effectively gutting a major section of the Voting Rights Act. In June, the court also struck down campaign finance restrictions limiting how much political parties may spend on candidates. Both decisions were split 6-3 along ideological lines.

As a result, she said, “both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting equality”.
Kagan said that decision was pushing political candidates “away from the center, toward the wings, toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about any more is being primaried”.

“It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she continued. “In this election, and the next election, we are seeing large states with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is very destructive to our democracy.”
Kagan also criticized the court’s decisions on campaign finance rules, and the increasing amounts of money in politics.
The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare. And they’re right.
Supreme court rebuffs Trump restrictions on medical care for trans inmates for now
The supreme court has refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately deny gender-affirming care for transgender people in federal prisons.

The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy while a legal challenge plays out. It was adopted after an executive order from Donald Trump, who’s taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.
Two of the supreme court’s six conservative justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, dissented, meaning they would have allowed the policy to be enforced.

Trump’s January 2025 executive order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex”.
The new policy would halt surgical and hormonal treatments, and end “social accommodations” like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.
Trans prisoners sued the administration over the policy and, so far, two lower courts have blocked officials from implementing the order as the larger lawsuit over the executive order continues.
Steve Witkoff lavished praise on Vladimir Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Trump’s special envoy told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.

The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war. More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.

The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.

Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting:
We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
A White House official has confirmed to the Guardian that Donald Trump’s roundtable at 2.30pm ET will be focused on cybercrime.

The president is “unleashing every available tool to stop foreign-based organized criminal organizations that exploit Americans in cyberspace”, the official said in a statement. “The most vulnerable among us – seniors, children, and low-income families – are disproportionately targeted, with scammers draining life savings, stealing the benefits of years of work, and destroying lives.”
According to the FBI, Americans reported losing almost $21bn to cybercrime and internet scams.
While Donald Trump will be in South Carolina today, his vice-president, JD Vance, will be stumping in Cincinnati, Ohio.

The Buckeye state is home to a must-keep Senate seat for Republicans, where the incumbent, John Husted, is fending off a challenge from former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown – the populist hoping for a comeback.

The state’s gubernatorial competition has also become increasingly bitter. On Tuesday, my colleague Chris Stein reported that the family of Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of Ohio, is criticizing her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy for using Acton’s estranged mother in a recently released campaign ad.
In the ad, which has circulated among conservatives on social media, Actons’s mother, Donna Arthur, said: “She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life.”

In a Tuesday statement, Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, said his sister is estranged from her mother, who had married a man that sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old. He added that Arthur remained in the marriage even after her husband was arrested and her children were taken away from her.

“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” he said in a statement released by Acton’s campaign.
Trump praises UK approval of controversial Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
Donald Trump has welcomed the news that UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.

“Great news for the wealth and prosperity of the United Kingdom, and the wonderful region of Aberdeen. The UK has started drilling in the North Sea, one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of OIL in the World,” the US president wrote on Truth Social.
He added that the UK should go “FULL BLAST”, and the move to resume offshore extraction would “make the UK very wealthy again”.

As my colleagues reported earlier today, Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, said the Jackdaw project will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter”. This comes after fierce opposition from several Labour MPs and environmental groups throughout the country.

Trump has long pushed for Britain to expand oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, instead of relying on wind turbines. He frequently clashed with Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, who argued that energy sustainability relied on renewable sources and moving away from fossil fuel dependence.

articles.headline: Miserable Man Utd ripped apart by Como
keyFacts: Manchester United lost 4-1 to Como in the UEFA Champions League, extending their winless streak to seven matches.
Manager Michael Carrick stated that he was really angry with the performance after his side was outworked in Italy.
Manchester United will next play Bournemouth at home in the Premier League on Sunday.
body: Como vs Manchester United; UEFA Champions League
Como vs Manchester United. UEFA Champions League.
Giuseppe Sinigaglia.
Como 4-1 Man Utd: Michael Carrick's side ripped apart in Italy during Champions League hammering

Match report as Nico Paz stars for Cesc Fabregas' Como as they take apart Manchester United; Michael Carrick's side now winless in seven games across all competitions after suffering Champions League humbling in Italy
Wednesday 21 October 2026 20:56, UK
Michael Carrick's Manchester United were ripped apart in a dreadful 4-1 defeat at Como in the Champions League, as their miserable run of results stretched to seven without a win.

The pressure continues to pile up on Carrick and this United side as their start to the season lurches from bad to worse - and on Wednesday night they were humbled by a Como team which delivered more intensity and quality in Italy.

The first attribute should be a non-negotiable but, despite United's application being in the spotlight, they were once again outworked by their opposition. Static in midfield, allowing Como players to run off them, losing markers... this was a shocking show of United's big failings out of possession.

The tone was set just two minutes in when Man Utd went behind early on - again. They are the first English side ever to concede in back-to-back Champions League games so soon and never got to grips with Cesc Fabregas' impressively coached team.
- As it happened | Teams | Stats
- Champions League fixtures and results | Latest news: Man Utd
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream Premier League games with no contract📺

Nico Paz brought the class for the hosts. The talented Argentina international stuck the opener into the top corner when Harry Maguire gave him too much space and then slotted in a third after catching Carlos Baleba in possession.
Paz set up another Como goal, too, playing in Tasos Douvikas, who ran away from a disoriented Matthijs de Ligt to find the net inside four minutes of the second half.

This was De Ligt's first start in 325 days due to back problems and came due to a wider spate of injuries at the club. But excuses for this United performance may wear thin quickly for the travelling support who stood in the pouring rain to watch this dismantling.

United's own star, Bruno Fernandes, was anonymous again, with just one goal involvement now in his past nine appearances for the club. His head-shaking summed up the mood before a sweeping Como fourth, which saw unmarked centre-back Jacobo Ramon head in, underline the vast gap between the sides on the night.

Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time goal was of little consolation. With just three points from their first three games, United have an uphill battle to make it out of the league phase in this competition. More immediately they are in desperate need of a better performance and win at home to Bournemouth on Sunday in the Premier League, live on Sky Sports.
Carrick 'really angry' with Man Utd performance
Manchester United boss Michael Carrick:

"I'm really angry but you've got to move on and deal with what's next. At this moment in time, there's a lot to do before the next game to get the team ready, because that was a difficult night for everybody.

"It's not about playing for me - it's about playing for this club. My whole life's wrapped around it [Man Utd]. I genuinely give everything I possibly can. It's not about me, it's about what we all give."
Asked if all of the players give as much as he does, Carrick said: "I'd like to think so. I didn't like what I saw tonight though."
Analysis: No shock to see Man Utd beaten
Sky Sports' Paul Merson:
"They've got to start winning matches. The problem with Manchester United is we still live in the age of when it was Rooney, Ronaldo and people like that.
"We're caught by the name - one of the biggest clubs in the world. But they're not one of the biggest teams in the world. They're far from it.

"Everybody judges them on when they had superstars. I don't see it as a shock. I look at their players and I don't go, 'oh this is a surprise'. I didn't expect them to beat Leeds. Absolutely not. I didn't expect them to beat Como. That's where they are.
"Rooney, Ronaldo, Keane... they're a million miles away."
Alarming stats for Man Utd
- Manchester United are winless in seven consecutive games in all competitions (D3 L4) for the first time since a run of eight matches between November and December 2015.
- Manchester United are the first English team ever to concede inside the opening two minutes of back-to-back major European games (47 seconds vs Atlético Madrid, 118 seconds vs Como).
- Como completed 594 passes tonight, the most by a team in a UEFA Champions League game against Manchester United since Barcelona in April 2019 (725).
Key moments from Como...
2: BIG MISS! Diogo Dalot takes a Matheus Cunha cross down in the box but his left-foot shot flashes wide of the far post.
2: GOAL! Nico Paz curls Como's opener into the top corner after Harry Maguire gives him too much space. A similar chance to Dalot's - a different result!
17: WIDE! Harry Maguire heads wide from a Bryan Mbeumo cross.
39: BIG MISS! Tasos Douvikas blazes over after stepping into the United box, failing to capitalise on static defending.
41: OFFIDE! A let-off for Senne Lammens and Man Utd as an offside flag goes up against Douvikas after he is brought down in the box by the goalkeeper.
HT: SUBS! Michael Carrick makes two changes at the break with Amad Diallo and Carlos Baleba sent on for Andrey Santos and Matheus Cunha.
49: GOAL! Man Utd concede at the start of the second half, too, as Paz plays in Douvikas, who runs off Matthijs de Ligt before firing in.
54: CLOSE! Lucas da Cunha blasts a left-foot shot wide from inside the box when he looked primed to add a third.
57: GOAL! Baleba makes an ill-advised turn in his own half with no cover behind him and Paz takes the ball and races in on goal to add a third.
64: CHANCES! But Amad can't connect with Fernandes' clipped pass into the box to pull one back for United. Moments later he sees a shot tipped over.
76: GOAL! Centre-back Jacobo Ramon heads in to finish off another sweeping Como move.
90+1: GOAL! Joshua Zirkzee is narrowly onside to grab a late goal for Man Utd, finding the net after controlling Amad's cross.

articles.headline: Pope Leo requires no further treatment after lung surgery, doctors say
keyFacts: Doctors confirmed Pope Leo XIV requires no further treatment following surgery for localized lung cancer.
The 71-year-old pontiff had surgery earlier this month at a Rome hospital to remove an early-stage lung nodule.
Pope Leo XIV has returned to public duties and stated he will gradually resume his activities.
body: Pope Leo XIV will not need further treatment following lung cancer surgery, his doctors said Wednesday.
The Vatican’s press office released an update from the pontiff’s doctors, saying final reports and analyses of tissue removed from his surgery were completed Wednesday.
Pope Leo rides popemobile for first time since surgery
“The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized,” said his doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora.
“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the statement said.
The 71-year-old had surgery earlier this month at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital to remove a lung nodule found during recent routine medical tests. Leo said the nodule was detected “at a very early stage.”
He was discharged on Saturday and returned to his public duties on Sunday with a prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica.
“This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are experiencing illness and a condition of frailty,” he said, thanking well-wishers.
Leo said that “having come through this delicate phase, as you know, I will now gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers.”

articles.headline: Bruno Fernandes rips into Michael Carrick’s tactics in bombshell comments after Man United defeat

body: Bruno Fernandes has effectively thrown Michael Carrick under the bus.

The Manchester United skipper, who walked off the field shaking his head after being substituted in the 66th minute, publicly questioned Carrick’s tactics immediately after a 4-1 loss to Como on Wednesday evening.
Fernandes didn’t hold back in his verdict on Carrick’s game plan Getty
What did Bruno Fernandes say about Michael Carrick?

“It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” Fernandes told TNT Sports.
When pressed on whether he insinuated Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes replied: “That’s on the manager and staff to see, not me.
“Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.
“As you saw with them [Como], the centre-back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.
“A team that plays through the middle with small connections, if you give them too much time and space then they can hurt you out wide.”

In response to Fernandes’ comments, Carrick said: “There’s a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you aren’t going to win.”
Fernandes’ staggering outburst comes one week after teammate Lisandro Martinez took a swipe at United technical director Jason Wilcox.

In the aftermath of United’s 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid, Martinez ‘100 per cent expected more’ from Wilcox in terms of strengthening the squad after Carrick steered them to a third-place finish last term.
Did Michael Carrick ignore his own players?

articles.headline: South Korea unveils world's first fielded laser air defense weapon — Hanwha's Cheongwang downs drones in 1 second for just $1.50 a shot
keyFacts: South Korea deployed the Cheongwang laser air defense system to destroy hostile drones without using conventional ammunition.
Manufacturer Hanwha Systems estimated that each engagement costs approximately $1.50.
Hanwha is pursuing international sales and developing more powerful mobile laser systems following the deployment.
body: - South Korea deploys Cheongwang, a laser weapon designed to destroy hostile drones
- Hanwha estimates each Cheongwang engagement costs approximately $1.50
- Laser weapons could reduce dependence on expensive interceptor missiles against drones
South Korea has deployed Cheongwang, a laser-based air defence system designed to destroy hostile drones without using conventional ammunition.
Developed by Hanwha Systems alongside the Agency for Defense Development, the weapon has entered operational service.
Its manufacturer estimates each engagement costs approximately $1.50, potentially reducing the financial burden of defending against inexpensive aerial threats.
Cheongwang demonstrates low-cost drone interception
The Republic of Korea Army tested Cheongwang during its TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise on October 14, 2026.
Hanwha Systems reported that the 30-kilowatt-class weapon destroyed all three drones launched during the exercise, which attracted about 500 military personnel and other observers.
Cheongwang operates by directing concentrated laser energy onto an aerial object until the resulting heat damages its structure or critical components.
Unlike conventional interceptors, the system does not require a separate missile for every engagement, provided sufficient electrical power and cooling remain available.

The manufacturer estimates that firing costs approximately $1.50 per engagement, substantially below the price of many missiles used against attack drones.
That figure does not necessarily represent the complete operating cost, since maintenance, electricity, equipment depreciation and other expenses may also affect deployment economics.

The conflicts between Russia and Ukraine as well as that between the U.S. / Israel and Iran have revealed how expensive drone interception can be. The laser technology seeks to offer a cheaper option.
“Laser weapons are core assets that will fundamentally change the game of air defense,” said Joohun Shin, head of Hanwha Systems' Laser Systems Business Centre
“Driven by unmatched technological capability and proven operational performance, we will accelerate our entry into the global market...”
Hanwha pursues more powerful mobile laser systems
Hanwha also demonstrated a 50-kilowatt Laser Armored Vehicle during the Defense Drone Technology Exhibition on September 16, 2026.
The company reported that Cheongwang neutralised four drones and two uncrewed aircraft consecutively during that separate demonstration.
The more powerful vehicle is being developed for greater mobility and potential international sales, with Hanwha displaying it at MSPO in Kielce, Poland.
Its development indicates that South Korea's defence industry is pursuing laser systems with different power levels and deployment requirements.
The United Kingdom is also advancing similar technology through DragonFire, a directed energy weapon developed by MBDA, Leonardo and QinetiQ alongside the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory.
The system struck aerial targets during trials in Scotland's Hebrides in 2024, and British authorities are advancing plans for installation aboard a Royal Navy Type 45 destroyer.
Laser weapons could offer sustained protection against repeated drone attacks, although their effectiveness depends on available power, tracking accuracy, engagement time and atmospheric conditions.
A laser can engage only a limited number of targets simultaneously, making attack volume an important consideration for operational planners.
South Korea's deployment allows Hanwha to pursue global customers seeking less expensive counter-drone options.
However, wider adoption will depend on independently verifiable performance and operational reliability and evidence of effectiveness.

articles.headline: What’s ahead if the polls are right — or wrong
keyFacts: Polls show generic movement away from Republicans and toward Democrats ahead of the midterm elections, putting Republican House and Senate majorities in jeopardy.
If polls are inaccurate and Republicans retain the Senate, federal court appointees could be confirmed and impeachment trials would likely fail.
A major Republican loss could prompt a party shift toward Marco Rubio, while Democratic gains could lead to investigations against Donald Trump.
body: With less than two weeks until the midterm elections , things look bad for President Donald Trump ’s Republican Party . Generic polls show significant movement away from Republicans and toward Democrats since Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris by 50% to 48% two years ago.

Republicans seem doomed to lose their exceedingly narrow House majority, although redistricting by both parties over the past two years has reduced the number of competitive seats and will likely limit their losses.

More surprisingly, in view of the 2024 results, Republicans’ Senate majority seems in jeopardy, as Democrats have been leading in polls in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas, states that Trump carried easily three times.

And Democratic leads in two Southern states that have been seriously contested in each presidential cycle, Georgia and North Carolina, are so solid that Republicans have written them off as irretrievably lost.

Two questions remain unanswered. The first will be settled by the election results, although that could take weeks given Alaska’s ranked choice voting system and California’s breathtakingly slow counting of ballots in contested House races. The second will shape election analysts’ forecasts for at least the next two years.

The first question is whether polls are understating Republican support, as they did in the presidential cycles of 2016, 2020, and 2024. The second is whether the move away from Republicans and toward Democrats will turn out to be a realignment away from the rough partisan parity that has prevailed for more than 30 years.

Starting with the presidential election of 1992 and the congressional election of 1994, Democrats have won the presidency five times and Republicans four, while Republicans have won House majorities 12 times and Democrats five.

Only one presidential nominee, Barack Obama in 2008, has won more than 51% of the popular vote, and neither party has held more than 257 of the House’s 435 seats. Democrats held the 60 Senate seats needed to overcome a filibuster for just seven months, from July 2009 to February 2010; Republicans never reached that threshold.

Democratic majorities of that magnitude are at the high end of, or even a bit beyond, what current polling suggests. The party would be winning over some who had been voting regularly for Trump and Republicans or benefiting from those individuals not voting at all.

And it would be winning just enough support to prevail in a solid majority of what look to be very close races. That is not so surprising, since Senate elections tend to be decided on national issues, and often all the close ones go one way.

But it’s also possible that polls are misleading. In past years, RealClearPolitics analyst Sean Trende has argued, polls have overstated Democrats’ chances in Republican states and vice versa. This year, the close races are on Republican turf, and if the polls prove to misfire that way again, Democratic gains may turn out to be minimal.

Republicans could hold on to a Senate majority in that case. That means Trump appointees to federal courts, including the Supreme Court, could be confirmed, and impeachment trials would likely go nowhere.

What about the consequences farther out, specifically for 2028? Minimal losses for Republicans might lead to a presidential endorsement and nomination of Vice President JD Vance. The risks of damage from Trump’s personal preoccupations — from tariffs to the triumphal arch — may seem less serious than the risks of outright rebellion against a leader eager to punish anything less than full devotion.

But a “thumping” — George W. Bush’s term for his party’s repudiation in 2006 — could leave many Republicans wondering whether the party needs, after a decade of domination by Trump, to take a different course. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s erudite speeches in February in Munich and this month in Athens, combined with his careful defenses of administration foreign policy, provide an alternative approach that chastened Republicans might prefer.

Democrats can be counted on, however great or minimal their gains, to pepper Trump and those around him with investigations, to stage votes for impeachment, and — if they have a Senate majority — to block confirmation of a Supreme Court nominee or any federal judge at all.

But they also face their own sharp divisions. Their lack of any articulate domestic platform leaves them open to members of the Democratic Socialists of America pushing radical and potentially unpopular measures such as “Medicare for all” — under which workers who like their health insurance can’t keep it. On foreign policy, they will probably try to hobble military operations against Iran and, with Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) looking over his shoulder at Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), may try to block military cooperation with Israel.

The result of one Senate contest in particular, the race in Michigan, may affect the course forward. There, Democratic nominee Abdul el Sayed has led Republican Mike Rogers in every public poll since late September, but in only one of eight polls by more than 2 percentage points. A polling error would not be shocking in Michigan, and while el Sayed went into the August primary with a 50% to 40% polling lead, he beat the more centrist Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) by only 48.4% to 47.6% in actual votes.

Republican Mike Rogers has led in only three of 29 public polls conducted since the August primary, but el Sayed’s average lead has narrowed from 48% to 44% in August and September to 47% to 46% in October. El Sayed’s perhaps surprising refusal to repudiate the Muslim Brotherhood or to say whether he considers Iran or Israel the greatest threat to the United States has evidently not strengthened his appeal.

A victory for the articulate el Sayed would make him a national leader of “progressive” Democrats. An el Sayed defeat would give Republicans a seat held by Democrats since 1978 and might convince many Democrats and some in the press that Medicare for all at home and opposition to Israel abroad are not a formula for their party’s success.

And what of the prospects for realignment beyond 2028? You could argue that it seems to be on schedule, perhaps overdue. The 1992 presidential and 1994 congressional elections were propelled by Bill Clinton and Newt Gingrich, both baby boomers by the definitions in Strauss and Howe’s Generations .

The seven presidents in the previous 40 years, all with military service in World War II, were born between 1911 and 1924. The five presidents since, three of them born in 1946 and the other two in 1942 and 1961, had no military service except for George W. Bush’s in the Texas Air National Guard.
HAS TRUMP BROKEN HIS MCDONALD’S PROMISE?

Starting in the 1990s, the South became the electoral heartland of the Republican Party, and the Northeast and Pacific coasts became the electoral heartlands of the Democratic Party. Starting in the 1990s and accelerating after Trump’s first run, Democrats have made gains among the affluent and college educated, and Republicans among blue-collar workers and non-college graduates.

Few predicted these trends, established politicians tried to buck them, and many thoughtful citizens haven’t absorbed them yet. I’d like to say I’ll describe what happens next, but having started writing for publication about these things in 1963, I’m not sure I’ll be in a position to do so. Perhaps answers will come from Marco Rubio, born in 1971; JD Vance and Abdul el Sayed, both born in 1984; and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, born in 1989.

articles.headline: What Christina Applegate’s misdiagnosis reveals about MS
keyFacts: Actor Christina Applegate announced she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2021, and doctors still do not know what causes her symptoms.
A cited meta-analysis indicates that roughly 15 percent of multiple sclerosis diagnoses may actually be false positives.
Experts say updated 2024 diagnostic criteria, expert MRI reviews, and spinal fluid testing can help ensure accurate diagnoses.
body: Christina Applegate at the 2023 Screen Actors Guild awards. | Valerie Macon/AFP via Getty Images

Christina Applegate, the actor who has been one of the most visible faces of multiple sclerosis since her 2021 diagnosis, made a stunning revelation this week: She does not have MS after all. And her doctors still don’t know what is causing her debilitating symptoms.
“I’m back at square one,” Applegate told fellow actor Jamie Lynn Sigler, who does have MS, on Sigler’s podcast MeSsy . “I was not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

It is a harrowing predicament for Applegate, and hopefully her medical team is able to get her the diagnosis and treatment she needs. But the fact is, her experience is not unique. Even as more and more Americans get diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, misdiagnosis remains all too common. According to one meta-analysis, roughly 15 percent of MS diagnoses may actually be false positives .

How could such a common medical condition — roughly 1 million Americans are living with the disease, about one in every 350 people — remain such a mystery? After Applegate’s announcement, I called some leading experts on MS to ask why diagnosing the disease is such a challenge, and what they want people to know. Here’s what I learned.
Why MS can be challenging to diagnose

Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune condition: The body mistakenly attacks cells meant to protect your brain and spinal cord, and the resulting damage interrupts nerve signals and causes the disease’s telltale symptoms of motor impairment, tingling sensations, and vision problems. Some people experience a rollercoaster of relapses and remissions; others see the disease steadily progress, eventually leading to serious disability.

The reality is, scientists still don’t really know what causes MS to develop, said Dr. Andrew Solomon , a neurologist at the University of Vermont who specializes in MS. Smoking is a known risk factor. Obesity and metabolic problems play a role, but we need more research. Even the precise role of genetics remains something of a mystery. “We don’t really know what causes or triggers the autoimmune response in any given individual,” Solomon said.
And that’s where the challenge in diagnosing it begins.

First, the testing can be imprecise; there is not a single test that reliably diagnoses MS. If a doctor suspects their patient may have MS, they usually undergo an MRI, which their physicians then scour for lesions that are typically associated with the disease. But those scans are still subject to interpretation: Other rare conditions sometimes resemble MS in imaging, as can diseases of blood vessels in the brain. You can also receive a spinal fluid analysis to check for abnormalities in your immune system, which the vast majority of MS patients have.

The nature of MS symptoms adds to the difficulty. They can often be vague early on: brain fog or fatigue or a general malaise. The tingling or vision problems can be similar to symptoms for other conditions that are not MS, and they are easily dismissed if they go into temporary remission, as often happens during the initial phases of the disease.

“Neurological symptoms sometimes can be vague — numbness, pins and needles — and it’s usually short-lived,” Dr. Saud Sadiq , chief research scientist and director of the Tisch Multiple Sclerosis Research Center of New York, told me. “Unless they’re taken seriously initially, they may be ignored because by the time the patient goes through the healthcare system and is actually referred to a neurologist, the symptoms have abated.”
If your doctor is diagnosing you with MS, ask directly: What’s the evidence?
One 2025 study by Solomon and his colleagues found that 40 percent of people who had later been d iagnosed with multiple sclerosis were initially misdiagnosed with a different disease.
“Because it’s so heterogeneous, it doesn’t present in the same way in everybody and can have varying severity, it can be hard to diagnose sometimes,” Solomon said.

Lastly, when people are experiencing debilitating symptoms, there is pressure to deliver some diagnosis — and that may push some doctors to leap to MS even if they are not sure, Solomon said. The recent advent of effective treatments that help manage the disease’s symptoms, especially when it is caught early, may add to that pressure, even if the better course would be to continue monitoring the person before they start a medication.

“There may be a lot of clinicians who, if they can’t find a better explanation than MS, may be inclined to diagnose MS, even if they don’t really meet our diagnostic criteria, because they’re worried about missing a window of opportunity to treat somebody,” Solomon said.

There is reason to hope the MS misdiagnosis problem could get better. The National Multiple Sclerosis Society released new diagnostic criteria in 2024 that Solomon said more physicians should become familiar with to better distinguish MS from problems like migraines or vascular disease. And because imaging is involved in diagnosis, there is optimism that AI could be a powerful new tool in delivering more accurate results.
What everyone should know about MS symptoms and diagnosis

The good news is that MS, when diagnosed properly, is a treatable condition these days. “The prognosis with new drugs is extremely good for long-term care,” Sadiq told me. “If patients stick to treatment at a good MS center, you can look forward to a life without disability in 2026.”

So it is worth being vigilant and talking to your doctor if you experience any concerning symptoms. You should seek care if you have numbness or pins and needles that persists for more than 24 to 48 hours, Sadiq said, or have motor problems, like one hand won’t work as you try to play piano. Dr. Annette Langer-Gould , who develops and evaluates programs for MS care at Kaiser Permanente, said numbness in your abdomen, chest or back, as opposed to your extremities, is a particular cause for concern. If one eye has normal vision and the other is blurred, that’s another good reason to get checked out.

If you do get tested, make sure the actual images of your MRIs end up being reviewed by an expert in MS. “The most common reasons the disease is still misdiagnosed are related to the providers’ lack of expertise usually in reading MRI scans,” Langer-Gould said. The spinal tap may sound scary, and doctors sometimes don’t recommend them because their insurance reimbursement is low — but they add to the confidence of a diagnosis. They are worth it, she said.
“American patients are very afraid of the spinal tap,” Langer-Gould said. “My message to patients is: Listen, just get the spinal. This way we’ll be sure.”

And do not be afraid to seek a second opinion for such a serious diagnosis, Sadiq added. Every state has a recognized MS center . If your doctor is diagnosing you with MS, ask directly: What’s the evidence? If your doctor is recommending that you start treatment, it could also be worth checking whether they have a relationship with a pharmaceutical company that affects how you perceive their judgment, Langer-Gould said.

People who have already been diagnosed may also be shaken by the Applegate news and question whether their own diagnosis might be wrong. Solomon said that folks should have a frank conversation with their physician about how exactly their case met the diagnostic criteria. With proper imaging and the spinal fluid tests, you can get to a confident diagnosis for the vast majority of people. But be your own advocate to make sure you’re satisfied.
“For many people, the diagnosis actually can be very straightforward,” Solomon said. “We really have no question about what it is.”

articles.headline: Kurt Suzuki out as Angels manager after 100-loss season, creating MLB's third vacancy
keyFacts: Kurt Suzuki will not return as Los Angeles Angels manager following a franchise-record 100-loss season, the team announced Wednesday.
The Angels have offered Suzuki a position as a special assistant to remain within the organization.
The Angels now have one of three managerial vacancies in Major League Baseball, alongside the Houston Astros and Seattle Mariners.
body: Kurt Suzuki will not return as manager of the Los Angeles Angels, the team announced Wednesday. Suzuki had a club option for 2027 in his contract. He has been offered a special assistant position to remain in the organization. The 2026 season was Suzuki's only season as manager. He guided the Halos to a franchise record 100 losses, not that they were expected to contend.

"Kurt has earned tremendous respect in our clubhouse, and I've seen firsthand how much he cares about our players," interim GM John Mozeliak said in a statement. "I do not believe our record this year was a true reflection of his abilities as a manager. I'm pleased we were able to offer Kurt a role to stay on as a special assistant, where his knowledge of our players and his perspective would continue to be valuable to the organization."

Suzuki, 43, was a special assistant to former Angels GM Perry Minasian from 2023-25 before taking over the managerial role this season. He had no prior coaching or managerial experience and the Angels gave him just a one-year contract, which is very unusual for a manager. Minasian was fired in June and replaced on an interim basis by Mozeliak.

"We haven't really dove deep into it," Suzuki told The Athletic in September when asked about his future and his conversations with Mozeliak. "We've had really good conversations about philosophies and stuff like that. We haven't really talked about next steps ... Would I like to be here? Of course I would."

. Mozeliak has expressed an interest in taking over the team's baseball operations on a permanent basis, though he remains the interim right now. It is likely that position will be filled before the Angels look for a new manager.

Whoever replaces Suzuki will be the team's fifth full-time manager in six years, joining Joe Maddon (2020-22), Phil Nevin (2022-23), Ron Washington (2024-25), and Suzuki (2026). Bench coach Ray Montgomery managed the final 88 games of the 2025 season while Washington was away from the team with a medical issue.
Fallen Angels
The Angels have had five managers in the last six seasons and have lost at least 85 games in each

The Angels lost 100 games for the first time in franchise history in 2026. They have not been to the postseason since 2014 or won a postseason game since 2009. Both are the longest droughts in baseball.
Baseball's three managerial vacancies belong to AL West teams: Angels, Houston Astros, and Seattle Mariners.

articles.headline: Star Wars Battlefront 3 Reportedly In Development By EA’s Top Shooter Studios
keyFacts: EA announced that Apex Legends developer Respawn Entertainment and Battlefield maker DICE are collaborating on an unspecified project during corporate restructuring and layoffs.
Variety reported through multiple sources that the collaborative project between DICE and Respawn is Star Wars Battlefront 3, though EA did not officially confirm this title.
DICE previously developed two Star Wars Battlefront games for EA that were released in 2015 and 2017.
body: Included in the shocking news of EA's restructuring , which includes layoffs and the closure of BioWare , is a mention from the publisher that Apex Legends studio Respawn Entertainment and Battlefield maker DICE are collaborating on a project. According to a report, that project is a long-awaited sequel set in a galaxy far, far away.

Per Variety , which cites "multiple sources," the DICE and Respawn project is Star Wars Battlefront 3. While EA itself did not confirm this, the company's memo about the restructuring says that the studios' title will contribute to EA's goal of delivering a "shooter portfolio that unlocks growth."

EA specifically states that learnings from Battlefield 6's launch and live service will further that goal, while also announcing that Apex Legends will be expanded with new "gameplay modes" and "other new experiences."

As for the purported existence of Star Wars Battlefront 3, the timing coincides with a recent rumor that Lucasfilm Games was seeking a development partner for a new Battlefront , and that DICE and Sony-owned studio Bungie were among the studios being considered.

DICE had made two Star Wars Battlefront games for EA, which were released in 2015 and 2017. Battlefront 2 attracted criticism over loot boxes (remember when that was the hot controversy of the day?), but the game still proved to be massively popular . Last year, Battlefront 2 suddenly had a resurgence in players, with many hoping that it would ignite talks of a third Battlefront .

Outside of Battlefront and shooters, the Star Wars franchise has gained two new popular entries this year alone, with strategy game Star Wars Zero Company (which Respawn co-developed) and racing title Star Wars: Galactic Racer enjoying critical success.

articles.headline: Gavin Newsom gets brutal exit report card as 62% of California voters are begging for a new direction: poll
keyFacts: A new poll found that 62 percent of California registered voters rate Governor Gavin Newsom's overall performance as fair or poor.
Voters gave Newsom negative ratings on homelessness, housing, and taxes, while his spokesperson highlighted his past election victories.
In the upcoming gubernatorial race, Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 55 percent to 35 percent among likely voters, the poll found.
body: Gavin Newsom is leaving Sacramento with a damning report card.

A new poll finds 62% of California registered voters rate his tenure fair or poor, with voters panning his handling of homelessness, housing, taxes, state spending and AI — and nearly two-thirds wanting the next governor to take the state in a new direction.
Just 36% gave Newsom’s overall performance an excellent or good rating in the survey conducted by TrueDot in collaboration with UC Berkeley’s Citrin Center and Politico.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Thanks for signing up!
The biggest group — 39% — rated his performance poor. Only 11% called it excellent.
The verdict was especially harsh on homelessness, where 72% said Newsom had handled the issue not too well or not at all well. Just a quarter offered a positive assessment.
Even voters in his own party gave him poor marks: Among Democrats and Democratic-leaning voters, 57% rated his handling of homelessness negatively.
Some 69% of voters rated Newsom’s handling of housing negatively, compared with 28% who said he had handled it well. That included 52% of Democrats and Democratic leaners giving him low marks.

Newsom spokesperson Izzy Gardon responded with a decidedly sunnier assessment, citing his electoral victories that included defeating a recall in 2021 and passing Proposition 50, last year’s congressional gerrymandering vote.

“Gavin Newsom overwhelmingly won five elections in eight years and is the most popular outgoing governor in the history of PPIC polling the question,” Gardon wrote in a text message to the California Post. “It’s a shame America’s Favorite Governor can’t run for another term — he’d crush it!”

Asked whether California’s next governor should generally continue Newsom’s policies or take the state in a different direction, 62% chose a change of course. Just 28% wanted Newsom’s policies to continue, while 10% were unsure.
Even among Democrats and Democratic leaners, fewer than half (49%) wanted the next governor to generally continue his policies. Another 37% preferred a different direction.

“Gov. Newsom frequently spins us around by saying California has the fourth largest economy in the world and has many firsts,” said Corrin Rankin, chairwoman of the California Republican Party. “But the reality of Newsom’s record of firsts are being number one in the country for the worst poverty, unemployment, cost-of-living, fraud, housing availability, income inequality and standardized test scores.”
Rankin blamed Newsom for students’ low test scores and college graduates being unable to “afford homes, pay their bills or get good jobs.”
“When 62% of Californians are unsatisfied with him, it’s easy to see that his presidential aspirations will be taking a ride on California’s high-speed rail to nowhere,” Rankin said.
Independents and other voters were more emphatic: 76% wanted a change, compared with just 11% who favored continuing Newsom’s approach.

Voters also gave Newsom poor marks on taxes and spending: Sixty percent rated his handling of taxes negatively, while 35% gave him positive marks. On state spending, over half offered a negative assessment and 39% a positive one.

Newsom also received negative marks on artificial intelligence regulation, with 43% saying he had handled the issue poorly, compared with 35% who said he had handled it well. Nearly a quarter were unsure.
Climate change supplied the lone bright spot. Half of voters said Newsom had handled the issue well, compared with 40% who disagreed.
Voters’ frustration with Newsom hasn’t translated into support for a Republican successor.
Democrat Xavier Becerra led Republican Steve Hilton 55% to 35% among likely voters, with 10% undecided.
Becerra’s campaign, which was endorsed by the current governor, did not respond to requests for comment on how his administration would differ from Newsom’s.
HiIton told The Post that poll findings show the last 16 years under Democratic governors — Newsom and former Gov. Jerry Brown — have been a “massive failure” and voters want change.

“The only way to get change is to vote for me as governor. Becerra would be four more years of one-party rule — but even worse than Newsom,” Hilton said. “He wouldn’t push back on any of the costs and craziness coming out of Sacramento. For everyone who is desperate for change and may be reluctant to vote Republican, I would say: Just try it.”
The online voter survey interviewed 1,149 California registered voters in English and Spanish from Oct. 9–14, including 909 likely voters.
The survey also exposed a gap between ordinary voters and the participating “policy influencers,” who were surveyed separately.

A separate survey of 213 influencers — who include political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers and others dialed in to California politics, according to Politico — found they were more likely to back Newsom’s performance as governor.

Among those insiders, 52% rated Newsom’s overall performance excellent or good — compared with 36% of voters. They were also substantially more positive about his handling of taxes and climate change.
But even that crowd had its limits: 52% wanted California’s next governor to take a different direction.
